The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$ C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}. $$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$ X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1, $$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$ \Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}). $$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$ N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}. $$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$ \ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right]. $$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$ \widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases} $$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], the independent prior coordinates and independent normal errors can be realized on countable product probability spaces. Fix one coordinate and put $s_i=i^{-r}$. By [F4], [F9] and [F11], the prior and sampling densities with respect to Lebesgue measure are $g_i(t)=(2\pi s_i)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/(2s_i)},\qquad q_i(x\mid t)=\sqrt{\frac n{2\pi}}e^{-n(x-\kappa_i t)^2/2}.$ Their product has exponent $-\tfrac12[(s_i^{-1}+n\kappa_i^2)t^2-2n\kappa_ixt+nx^2]$. Completing the square in $t$ gives conditional variance $v_i=(s_i^{-1}+n\kappa_i^2)^{-1}$ and conditional mean $m_i(x)=v_i n\kappa_i x$. Integrating the same product over $t$ gives the prior-predictive density $\frac{\exp\{-x^2/[2(n^{-1}+\kappa_i^2s_i)]\}} {\sqrt{2\pi(n^{-1}+\kappa_i^2s_i)}}.$ This is the density of $N(0,n^{-1}+\kappa_i^2s_i)$ by [F4], [F9] and [F11].

The scalar posterior densities in step 1.1 are probability densities by [F4], [F9] and [F11]. For each fixed data sequence, [F2] defines the product posterior measure $K(x,\cdot)$. On a finite-coordinate parameter cylinder $A$, $K(x,A)$ is a finite product of normal probabilities, hence is Borel in $x$. The scalar Bayes identity and independence of the coordinate pairs give the conditional-law identity for such $A$ and every finite-coordinate data cylinder. For fixed $A$, both sides, as functions of the data event, are finite measures; the scalar Bayes identity with the full data event shows that both have total mass equal to the prior probability of $A$. If that mass is positive, normalize both measures and apply [F6]; if it is zero, both measures are identically zero. The data cylinders generate the data sigma-algebra by [F3], so the identity holds for every data event. The class of parameter sets $A$ for which $K(\cdot,A)$ is Borel and the identity holds for every data event contains the parameter-cylinder $\pi$-system. It is a Dynkin system because complements use $1-K(x,A)$ and differences of finite measures, while countable disjoint unions use pointwise limits of measurable partial sums and countable additivity of the joint measures. A second use of [F3] and [F6] proves the identity for every product-measurable $A$. Therefore $K$ is a posterior probability kernel.

Write $a_i=n\kappa_i^2s_i$. The density of the marginal $N(0,n^{-1}(1+a_i))$ coordinate relative to $N(0,n^{-1})$ is $L_i(x_i)=(1+a_i)^{-1/2}\exp\{n a_i x_i^2/[2(1+a_i)]\}$. Since $\sum_i a_i\le nC^2\sum_i i^{-1-2\alpha-2p}<\infty$, [F5] and [F10] give $\sum_i a_i Z_i^2<\infty$ almost surely under $Q_{n,0}$, where $Z_i=\sqrt nX_i$. Hence $\sum_i|\log L_i(X_i)|<\infty$ there. Choose $J$ so $a_i<1$ for $i>J$. Direct Gaussian integration gives $E_{Q_{n,0}}L_i^2=(1-a_i^2)^{-1/2}$ for $i>J$, and $\prod_{i>J}(1-a_i^2)^{-1/2}<\infty$ because $\sum_i a_i^2<\infty$. The finite tail products are mean-one martingales and are Cauchy in $L^2$: for $m>k>J$, independence gives $E|\prod_{i=J+1}^{m}L_i-\prod_{i=J+1}^{k}L_i|^2 =E(\prod_{i=J+1}^{k}L_i^2)\{\prod_{i=k+1}^{m}(1-a_i^2)^{-1/2}-1\}$, which tends uniformly to zero as $k\to\infty$. The finite initial product is independent of the tail and has mean one, so multiplication preserves $L^1$ convergence. By absolute convergence of the log series, the nonnegative limit is $\prod_iL_i=\exp(\sum_i\log L_i)$ and has expectation one. It agrees with the marginal product law on every finite cylinder, so [F6] identifies it as $dQ_{n,\alpha}/dQ_{n,0}$. Taking logarithms and substituting $s_i=i^{-r}$ gives the displayed $\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.

Under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$, [F10] and the independence in the model give $E X_i^2=\kappa_i^2\theta_{0,i}^2+n^{-1}$. The sum $\sum_i a_i E(nX_i^2)$ is finite: its noise part is $\sum_i a_i$, and its signal part is $n^2\sum_i\kappa_i^4i^{-r}\theta_{0,i}^2 \le n^2C^4\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2<\infty$. Thus the same absolute-convergence bound for $\sum_i|\log L_i(X_i)|$ holds under the true sampling law.

By [F5] and [F10], the prior has expected squared norm $\sum_i i^{-r}<\infty$, hence belongs to $\ell^2$ almost surely. The posterior variances satisfy $\sum_i v_i\le\sum_i i^{-r}<\infty$. For its mean, write $m_i(X_i)=w_i\theta_{0,i}+ \sqrt n\kappa_i(i^r+n\kappa_i^2)^{-1}Z_i$, where $w_i=n\kappa_i^2/(i^r+n\kappa_i^2)\le1$. The cross term has mean zero because $E Z_i=0$ by [F10], so $E_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\sum_i m_i(X_i)^2 \le \sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2+ nC^2\sum_i i^{-2r-2p}<\infty.$ Therefore the posterior mean is in $\ell^2$ almost surely; for almost every such observation its posterior expected squared norm is $\sum_i(m_i(X_i)^2+v_i)<\infty$, so the posterior gives $\ell^2$ mass one.

$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.

$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by

Use the defined inverse Gaussian sequence procedure with fixed $p,C,L_0,N_0,\rho$ and $0<A=A_n\le\sqrt{\log n}/(4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)})$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Write
$$ r_\alpha=1+2\alpha+2p,\quad s_\alpha=1+2\alpha,\quad N_\alpha=n^{1/r_\alpha},\quad V_\alpha=N_\alpha\log N_\alpha,\quad f_\alpha(i)=\frac{n^2i^{s_\alpha}\log i}{(i^{r_\alpha}+n)^2},\quad S_\alpha=\sum_i f_\alpha(i)\theta_i^2,\quad h_\alpha=S_\alpha/V_\alpha. $$

$$ E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le A}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha(1+h_\alpha)}\le\frac{K\{1+A L_0\rho^{1+2A}\log n\}}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0. $$

derivations.claim: Set $u=(16C^8)^{-1}$ and $v=8C^8$. Continuity of $h_n$ implies $h_n\le u$ on $[0,\underline\alpha_n]$ whenever $\underline\alpha_n>0$, and $h_n\ge v$ on $[\overline\alpha_n,A]$ whenever $\overline\alpha_n<A$. These implications include the empty-set conventions. Moreover $\underline\alpha_n\le\overline\alpha_n$: otherwise any point strictly between them would have $h_n<u$ by the first-infimum definition and $h_n>v$ by the last-supremum definition, a contradiction. At a nontrivial threshold, continuity gives $h_n(\underline\alpha_n)\ge u$ if $\underline\alpha_n<A$ and $h_n(\overline\alpha_n)\le v$ if $\overline\alpha_n>0$.

Write $V_\alpha=N_{n,\alpha}\log N_{n,\alpha}$. The expectation bounds in F2 imply $E M_n/V_\alpha\ge1/(16C^4)$ when $h_n\le u$, and $E M_n/(V_\alpha h_n)\le-5/(8C^4)$ when $h_n\ge v$. Therefore $E M_n/[V_\alpha(1+h_n)]$ has a positive margin at least $1/(32C^4)$ on the lower interval and a negative margin of magnitude at least $1/(32C^4)$ on the upper interval. For a nonnegative variable $Y$, integrating $\varepsilon\mathbf1_{\{Y>\varepsilon\}}\le Y$ proves $P(Y>\varepsilon)\le EY/\varepsilon$. The uniform centered-score bound and this inequality show that, uniformly in polished-tail truths, with probability tending to one the likelihood derivative is positive throughout the lower interval and negative throughout the upper interval. Integration shows strict increase and decrease, including comparisons with the interval endpoints. Every global maximizer lies in the asserted bracket, proving the first conclusion.

For an arbitrary square-summable truth with $\underline\alpha_n>0$, the lower interval still has $h_n\le u$. Apply the final, arbitrary-truth bound in F2 to $[0,\underline\alpha_n]$ with $H=u$. The positive expectation margin $1/(16C^4)$ is unchanged. Markov's inequality makes the derivative positive throughout that interval with probability tending to one uniformly in all such truths. Thus no global maximizer lies below $\underline\alpha_n$. If this endpoint is zero, the conclusion holds automatically.

If $\underline\alpha_n=A$ or $\overline\alpha_n=0$, their ordering forces equality of both endpoints and the rate ratio is one. Otherwise apply F2's kernel comparison at $a=\underline\alpha_n$, $b=\overline\alpha_n$. Step 1.1 gives $u\le(4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A})(N_b/N_a)v$, hence $N_a/N_b\le128C^{16}(4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A})$. All constants and probability bounds are uniform in the specified classes.

$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$ C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}. $$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$ X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1, $$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$ \Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}). $$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$ N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}. $$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$ \ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right]. $$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$ \widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases} $$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Use the inverse Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and $\kappa_i^2\in[C^{-2}i^{-2p},C^2i^{-2p}]$.
Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. Let
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ with $\theta_{0,1}=0$.
For $n\ge3$ and $\alpha\in[0,A]$, put
$$ N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/(1+2\alpha+2p)},\qquad h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)= \frac{1+2\alpha+2p}{N_{n,\alpha}\log n} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2 i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_{0,i}^2} {(i^{1+2\alpha+2p}+n)^2}. $$
Define
$$ \underline\alpha_n= \inf\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\ge(16C^8)^{-1}\}, \qquad \overline\alpha_n= \sup\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\le8C^8\}, $$
with the source conventions $\inf\varnothing=A$ and $\sup\varnothing=0$.
Then the source bracket result is
$$ \inf_{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho),\,\theta_{0,1}=0} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)} \bigl(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n\le\overline\alpha_n\bigr) \longrightarrow1. $$
More generally, the same conclusion holds with $A=A_n$ whenever
$$ 0<A_n\le\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}} $$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Uniformly in the polished-tail class, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$ \frac{n^{-2\underline\alpha_n/(1+2\underline\alpha_n+2p)}}{n^{-2\overline\alpha_n/(1+2\overline\alpha_n+2p)}}\le\left[128C^{16}\{4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A_n}\}\right]^{1+2p}. $$
In particular, for fixed $A$ the two rates are uniformly comparable. The lower bracket alone is valid uniformly over arbitrary $\theta_0\in\ell^2$, using the same definition of $\underline\alpha_n$ and the same procedure/domain hypotheses:
$$ \inf_{\theta_0\in\ell^2}P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n)\longrightarrow1. $$

In the defined inverse Gaussian procedure, let $\theta=(\theta_i)\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the true sequence. For $n\ge3$ and $\alpha\in[0,A_n]$ write $q_\alpha=1+2\alpha+2p$, $N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/q_\alpha}$, $R_{n,\alpha}=N_{n,\alpha}^{-2\alpha}=N_{n,\alpha}^{1+2p}/n$, and
$$ h_n(\alpha;\theta):=\frac{q_\alpha}{N_{n,\alpha}\log n}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_i^2}{(i^{q_\alpha}+n)^2}. $$

$$ B_i(\alpha)=-\frac{i^{1+2\alpha}\theta_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad W_i(\alpha)=\frac{\sqrt n\kappa_i Z_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}. $$

Let $0\le a\le b\le A_n$, with $N_{n,A_n}\to\infty$ and $A_n/N_{n,A_n}\to0$. Constants below depend only on $p,C,L_0,\rho,\gamma$. Part (iii) also holds at $a=0$. At $b=0$ the procedure gives the whole parameter space whenever the selector lies in $[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: Write $a=a_n$, $b=b_n$. Continuity of $h_n(\cdot;\theta_0)$ gives $h_n(b;\theta_0)\le8C^8$ whenever $b>0$: if the sublevel set is nonempty, its supremum belongs to it by compactness, while an empty sublevel set has $b=0$ by convention. The hypotheses $N_{n,A_n}\to\infty$ and $A_n/N_{n,A_n}\to0$ in [F3] hold for fixed $A$ and under the growing cap, because $\log N_{n,A_n}=\log n/(1+2A_n+2p)$ grows at least as a positive multiple of $\sqrt{\log n}$ when $A_n$ is unbounded.

On the bracket event from [F2], the case $\widehat\alpha_n=0$ gives coverage by [F1]. Otherwise $b>0$. Couple the centered posterior-mean noise by the same normal errors for every $\alpha$. Each posterior variance decreases with $\alpha$, so its norm quantile decreases too, and [F3] gives $r(\widehat\alpha_n)\ge r(b)\ge\sqrt{dR_b}$. The triangle inequality and [F3] then give, with probability tending uniformly to one, $\|\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n}-\theta_0\|\le K_1(1+\rho^{1+2b+2p})\sqrt{R_b}+K_2\sqrt{R_a}$. The probability error for the noise is bounded by $K/N_{n,A_n}$ and is independent of the truth.

For fixed $A$, [F2] bounds $R_a/R_b$ by a constant depending only on the fixed parameters. Choose $L$ so that $L\sqrt d$ exceeds $K_1(1+\rho^{1+2A+2p})+K_2\sqrt{R_a/R_b}$ uniformly. Then step 1.2 implies coverage on an event whose probability tends uniformly to one. This proves the fixed-cap conclusion.

For growing $A_n$, the sharpened comparison in [F2] bounds $R_a/R_b$ by $K(1+L_0\rho^{1+2A_n})^{1+2p}$, with $K$ independent of $n$ and the truth. Hence $\sqrt{R_a/R_b}\le K_{\mathrm{noise}}\rho^{(1+2p)A_n}$ after absorbing fixed factors into $K_{\mathrm{noise}}$. The bias bound from step 1.2 is at most $K_{\mathrm{bias}}\rho^{2A_n}\sqrt{R_b}$, with $K_{\mathrm{bias}}$ also independent of $n$ and the truth. Since $(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$ dominates both $\rho^{(1+2p)A_n}$ and $\rho^{2A_n}$, choose a fixed $K_{\mathrm{infl}}\ge1$ with $K_{\mathrm{infl}}\sqrt d\ge K_{\mathrm{noise}}+K_{\mathrm{bias}}$. Then the bound on $L_n$ makes the credible radius at least the sum of the bias and noise bounds on the bracket and noise events. The bracket and noise errors tend uniformly to zero because $N_{n,A_n}\to\infty$, proving the growing-cap conclusion.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then

derivations.claim: The recursion gives $N_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}^2N_j$. The preceding last gap endpoint satisfies $\rho_{j-1}N_{j-1}\le N_j/(2\rho_j)<N_j$, while the next first gap begins at $N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}N_j>2N_j$. For the lower bound retain $i\le\lfloor N\rfloor$, replace the denominator by $4n^2$, and use $\sum_{i\le\lfloor N\rfloor}\log i\ge N\log N/2$ for $N\ge e^8$, obtained by integrating $\log x$. For the upper bound the terms below $N$ total at most $V$. The remaining terms are bounded by $n^2\sum_{i>N}i^{-2r}\log i$, which is at most $V\{(2r-1)^{-1}+[(2r-1)^2\log N]^{-1}+N^{-1}\}<2V$, by integrating $x^{-2r}\log x$ and including its value at $N$.

For a polished-tail truth put $m=\lceil N/\rho\rceil$, $B=\{m,\ldots,\lfloor\rho m\rfloor\}$ and $E_B=\sum_{i\in B}\theta_i^2$. On $B$ one has $N/\rho\le i\le N+\rho$, $\log i\ge\log N/2$ and $i^r+n\le3n$. Thus $S_\alpha\ge\rho^{-s}N^s(\log N)E_B/18$, and $\sum_{i>N}\theta_i^2\le L_0E_B$. For $i>N$, $f_\alpha(i)\log i\le n^2i^{-1-2\alpha-4p}(\log i)^2\le N^s(\log N)^2$, since the function on the right before evaluation at $N$ decreases beyond $N$. Below $N$, $\log i\le\log N$. Consequently $ \sum_i f_\alpha(i)(\log i)\theta_i^2\le(1+18L_0\rho^s)(\log N)S_\alpha. $ All these inequalities hold also when $S_\alpha=0$.

For every $i$, $f_\alpha(i)\le2N^s\log N$. Below $N$ use the denominator bound $n^2$; above $N$ write $i=Nx$ and $q=1+2\alpha+4p\ge1$, obtaining the upper bound $N^sx^{-q}(\log N+\log x)$, and use $x^{-q}\log x\le1/(eq)$. For $a\le b$ and $2\le i\le N_b$, $f_a(i)/f_b(i)=i^{-2(b-a)}[(i^{r_b}+n)/(i^{r_a}+n)]^2\le4$. Apply step 2.1 at $b$ to the energy above $N_b$, and the kernel supremum at $a$, to obtain $ S_a\le4S_b+36L_0\rho^{s_b}\frac{N_a^{s_a}\log N_a}{N_b^{s_b}\log N_b}S_b. $ Multiply by $V_b/V_a$. The identities $N_\alpha^{s_\alpha}=nN_\alpha^{-2p}$, $\log N_b/\log N_a\le1$ and $(N_b/N_a)^{2p}\le1$ give the stated comparison of $h_a,h_b$, without dividing by a possibly zero signal.

Differentiation under the signal sum is valid by domination by a bounded multiplier of $\theta_i^2$, since its tail and each of its first derivatives are bounded by a constant times $i^{-1-4p}(\log i)^k$. It gives $S_\alpha'=2\sum_i f_\alpha(i)(\log i)(n-i^{r_\alpha})/(n+i^{r_\alpha})\theta_i^2$. Step 2.1 bounds its absolute value by $2(1+18L_0\rho^{s_\alpha})(\log N_\alpha)S_\alpha$. Moreover $V_\alpha'/V_\alpha=-2(1+\log N_\alpha)/r_\alpha$. Therefore $G_\alpha=V_\alpha+S_\alpha$ is positive and continuously differentiable, with $|G_\alpha'|/G_\alpha\le K L_0\rho^{1+2A}\log n$.

Set $t_i=i^{1+2\alpha}\kappa_i^{-2}$ and $a_i=n^2t_i\log i/(t_i+n)^2$. Direct differentiation of finite likelihood sums, followed by centering, gives $ E_\theta M_n(\alpha)=\sum_i\frac{n^2\log i}{(t_i+n)^2}-\sum_i\frac{n^2i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_i^2}{(t_i+n)^2},\qquad Q_n(\alpha)=-\sum_i a_i(\alpha)(X_i^2-E_\theta X_i^2). $ Ellipticity compares $t_i+n$ to $i^{r_\alpha}+n$ with factors $C^{\pm2}$. Thus step 1.2 proves both asserted expectation inequalities. By [F4], $EZ_i=0$ and $EZ_i^2=1$. Two integrations by parts using $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ give $EZ_i^4=3$; the boundary terms vanish because every polynomial times $\phi$ tends to zero at infinity. Hence $E|Z_i|^3\le(EZ_i^2)^{1/2}(EZ_i^4)^{1/2}<\infty$ by [F3]. The density $\phi$ is even, so the integrable odd moment satisfies $EZ_i^3=0$. Expanding $X_i^2-E_\theta X_i^2$ now gives $\operatorname{Var}(X_i^2)=2/n^2+4\kappa_i^2\theta_i^2/n$. Independence makes variances additive. Finally $a_i'=2(\log i)a_i(n-t_i)/(n+t_i)$, so $|a_i'|\le2(\log i)a_i$.

For $j=0,1$ the preceding identities give $ \operatorname{Var}_\theta Q_n^{(j)}(\alpha)\le K N_\alpha(\log N_\alpha)^{2+2j}(1+h_\alpha). $ Here are the series estimates in full. The noise contribution is bounded by $K\sum_i[n i^{r_\alpha}/(i^{r_\alpha}+n)^2]^2(\log i)^{2+2j}$. Below $N$ bound the bracket by one; above $N$ bound it by $ni^{-r}$ and use step 1.1 with $q=2r-1\ge1$. The result is $KN(\log N)^{2+2j}$. The signal contribution is bounded by $K\sum_i f_\alpha(i)\theta_i^2[n i^r(\log i)^{1+2j}/(i^r+n)^2]$. The bracket is at most $K(\log N)^{1+2j}$: below $N$ this is immediate, and above $N$ it follows from $x^{-r}(\log N+\log x)^{1+2j}\le K(\log N)^{1+2j}$ for $x=i/N\ge1$, $r\ge1$. The signal contribution is therefore at most $KS_\alpha(\log N)^{1+2j}=KN(\log N)^{2+2j}h_\alpha$. This calculation uses only $\theta\in\ell^2$, not polished tails.

The random sums have common versions suitable for integration and suprema. On each fixed $[0,A]$, the variance-series tails for $Q_n,Q_n'$ tend to zero uniformly: coarse dominating summands are constants times $i^{-2-4p}(\log i)^4$ and $i^{-1-4p}(\log i)^4\theta_i^2$, both summable. For a finite centered tail $T$, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $E\sup|T|\le\sqrt{ET(0)^2}+\int_0^A\sqrt{ET'(u)^2}\,du$. Thus partial sums converge in expected uniform norm to a continuous $Q_n$. Their derivatives converge in $L^1(dP\,d\alpha)$, so the limit has absolutely continuous paths and the fundamental theorem passes to the limit. Deterministic expectation sums converge uniformly by the analogous kernel domination. Choose an almost surely uniformly convergent subsequence of score sums. On the procedure's full-probability domain, the finite likelihood sums converge at zero to its prescribed value. Integrating those finite scores and passing along this subsequence gives $\ell_n(\alpha)=\ell_n(0)+\int_0^\alpha M_n(u)\,du$ simultaneously on $[0,A]$. Its continuous integrand is therefore the asserted derivative, including the right endpoint derivative at zero.

Put $R_\alpha=Q_n(\alpha)/G_\alpha$. By step 3.2, $E|R_\alpha|\le K/\sqrt{N_\alpha}$. The quotient rule, step 2.3 and Cauchy–Schwarz give $E|R_\alpha'|\le K L_0\rho^{1+2A}(\log n)/\sqrt{N_\alpha}$. The absolutely continuous version from step 3.3 satisfies $\sup_{[0,A]}|R|\le|R_0|+\int_0^A|R_\alpha'|\,d\alpha$. Taking expectations by Tonelli and using $N_\alpha\ge N_A$ proves the first bound. For arbitrary truths on an interval where $h\le H$, instead normalize by $V$ alone. Step 3.2 and $|V'/V|\le3\log n$ yield $E|Q/V|\le K_H/\sqrt{N_A}$ and $E|(Q/V)'|\le K_H\log n/\sqrt{N_A}$. The same integral inequality proves the final asserted bound, including $c=0$.

Write $\lambda=\log(\rho\vee e)\ge1$ and $t=\sqrt{\log n}$. At the maximal allowed $A$, $2A\log\rho\le t\sqrt\lambda/2$, whereas $\tfrac12\log N_A=t^2/[2(1+2A+2p)]\ge t\sqrt\lambda-O(1)$. Consequently $\rho^{2A}/\sqrt{N_A}\le K\exp(-t\sqrt\lambda/2)$, which dominates every polynomial in $\log n$. The first bound tends to zero; the arbitrary-truth bound is smaller apart from a fixed factor. For smaller $A$, the numerators only decrease and $N_A$ increases. This proves all uniform convergence assertions.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$ C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}. $$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$ X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1, $$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$ \Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}). $$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$ N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}. $$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$ \ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right]. $$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$ \widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases} $$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, a sequence
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, a truth
$\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, and $0<\alpha<\infty$ in the
procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]]. Put
$r=1+2\alpha$. Then the product prior is supported on $\ell^2$, and its
posterior kernel under the prior-predictive law $Q_{n,\alpha}$ is the product
of the coordinate laws
$$ N\!\left( \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2}, \frac{1}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right),\qquad i\ge1, $$
For $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost every observation $x$, this same kernel is
supported on $\ell^2$, and its posterior mean belongs to $\ell^2$.

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and
$$ \log\frac{dQ_{n,\alpha}}{dQ_{n,0}}(x) =-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^r}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right] =\ell_n(\alpha;x). $$
The density identity and absolute convergence hold $Q_{n,0}$-almost surely.
The same displayed score series also converges absolutely
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

derivations.claim: The posterior coordinate variances satisfy $C^{-4}i^{2p}/(i^q+n)\le v_i\le C^4 i^{2p}/(i^q+n)$, and the noise weights satisfy $t_i=n\kappa_i^{-2}/(i^{1+2\alpha}\kappa_i^{-2}+n)^2\le C^6 n i^{2p}/(i^q+n)^2$. Split at $N$. For $i\le N$, $t_i\le C^6 i^{2p}/n$ and $\sum_{i\le N} i^{2p}\le2N^{1+2p}$ for $N\ge2$. For $i>N$, $t_i\le C^6 n i^{-2-4\alpha-2p}$; the decreasing-function integral comparison bounds its sum by $2C^6nN^{-1-4\alpha-2p}\le2C^6R$. Thus $\sum_i t_i\le4C^6R$ and $\sup_i t_i\le C^6R/N$. By [F4], $E Z_i^2=1$. Two integrations by parts using $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ give $E Z_i^4=3$ (all boundary terms vanish), so $\operatorname{Var}(Z_i^2)=2$. Independence then bounds the variance of $\sum_i t_iZ_i^2$ by $8C^{12}R^2/N$. Finite sums pass to the nonnegative infinite sum by monotone convergence; the centered sums are Cauchy in $L^2$ since $\sum_i t_i^2<\infty$.

All $t_i(\alpha)$ decrease in $\alpha$. Thus the same $Z_i$ couple the process and $\sup_{a\le\alpha\le b}\|W(\alpha)\|^2=\sum_i t_i(a)Z_i^2$. Chebyshev at threshold $R_a$ above its mean yields $P\{\sup\|W\|^2>(4C^6+1)R_a\}\le8C^{12}/N_a$, proving (iii).

For the posterior-radius lower bound, retain only integer indices $N/2\le i\le N$. For $N\ge6$ there are at least $N/3$ such indices, and each has $v_i\ge C^{-4}2^{-2p-1}N^{2p}/n$. The retained quadratic sum $U_*$ therefore has mean at least $d_0R$, where $d_0=C^{-4}2^{-2p-1}/3$. Each retained variance weight is at most $C^4N^{2p}/n=C^4R/N$, so $\operatorname{Var}U_*\le2(C^4R/N)E U_*$. Also $E U_*\le C^4R$, hence $P\{U_*<d_0R/2\}\le8C^8/(d_0^2N)$. Since the full posterior squared norm dominates $U_*$, for sufficiently large $N$ its $1-\gamma$ quantile is at least $d_0R/2$. This proves (i), with $d=d_0/2$, independently of $A_n$. The full norm is finite a.s. when $\alpha>0$ because $\sum v_i\le\sum i^{-1-2\alpha}<\infty$. At zero use only the defined whole-space branch.

Each squared bias coefficient increases with $\alpha$, so it suffices to consider $b$. Set $q=q_b$, $N=N_b$. By the bounds on $\kappa_i$, $\|B(b)\|^2\le C^8\sum_i i^{2+4b+4p}\theta_i^2/(i^q+n)^2$. For $2\le i\le N$ and $N\ge4$, $i^{q+2p}/\log i\le N^{q+2p}/\log N$. Indeed $x^r/\log x$ for $r\ge1$ has its maximum on $[2,N]$ at an endpoint, and its value at $N\ge4$ exceeds its value at $2$. The contribution of these indices is consequently at most $C^8R h_n(b;\theta)$. The index $1$ is zero by hypothesis.

Put $m=\lfloor N\rfloor$. For large $n$, $m\ge N_0$ and uniformly for $b\le A_n$, $m^{1+2b}\ge N^{1+2b}/2$ and $\log m\ge\log N/2$, because $(1+2A_n)/N_{A_n}\to0$. On the block $m\le i\le\lfloor\rho m\rfloor$, $i^q+n\le(\rho^q+1)n\le2\rho^q n$. Therefore $h_n(b;\theta)\ge N^{2b}\rho^{-2q}\sum_{i=m}^{\lfloor\rho m\rfloor}\theta_i^2/16$. The polished-tail inequality bounds $\sum_{i>N}\theta_i^2$ by $16L_0\rho^{2q}R h_n(b;\theta)$. Each actual bias coefficient has magnitude at most one, so this bounds the remaining squared bias. Together with step 3.1 and $h_n(b)\le8C^8$, this proves (ii).

boundaries.reason: Statement has a nonempty interval [a,b] because 0<=a<=b; its coordinate set is the fixed positive integers. The retained band in proof 2.2 is nonempty once N>=6, as the proof explicitly imposes.

boundaries.evidence: Statement allows theta=0, giving B=0 identically in its displayed formula. Part (iii) still bounds the nonzero Gaussian noise; proof 2.2 uses the procedure whole-space convention at b=0.

Statement fixes gamma in the procedure's interior credibility regime, so gamma=1 is not used as a quantile endpoint. The noise probability lower bound 1-K/N_a tends to one, but is not claimed to equal one at finite n.
For a=b the suprema in Statement reduce to a single regularity value. Proof 2.1's monotone coupling remains an equality; if h_n(b)=0 the bias bounds in 3.1–3.2 give zero without dividing by it.
Statement permits a=0, b=0 and a=b. Proof 2.1 establishes the noise bound at a=0; proof 2.2 imposes b>0 for posterior-radius finiteness and uses only the whole-space convention at zero.

Fact F1 supplies posterior coordinates on the AC-based procedure model. Proof 2.1 uses the already fixed same Z_i coupling for all alpha; the band retained in 2.1 is deterministic, so no new selection is required.

The Statement does not infer truth regularity from a radius or noise bound. In particular a small bias is not asserted to force the polished-tail inequality.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then

def-gaussian-sequence-hyperrectangle-cla.source_definition:
Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$ \Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}. $$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

def-polished-tail-class-for-gaussian-seq.source_definition:
Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$ \sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2. $$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-se.source_definition:
Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$ C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}. $$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$ X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1, $$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$ \Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}). $$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$ N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}. $$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$ \ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right]. $$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$ \widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases} $$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.
